e.t: Abram is a proper name—the personal name of the man identified in the Greek Old Testament as Abram. It refers to one individual rather than describing an action, quality, or object. The name appears 66 times across 52 verses in the Greek Old Testament, occurring 65 times in Genesis and once in Nehemiah. Its recorded use begins in Genesis 11:26 and ends in Nehemiah 9:7. In some sentences, the name may appear in a possessive expression such as “Abram’s,” but it still identifies Abram.

This LXX word is a proper name: “Agarēnos” or “Agarinos.” It identifies a named person or people rather than describing an action, quality, or object, though the lexical information does not identify which. It occurs twice in the Greek Old Testament corpus, once in 1 Chronicles 5:19 and once in Psalm 82:7. Its precise referent in either passage must be determined from the surrounding verse text.

Agia, also rendered Ayia, is a proper name in the Greek Old Testament and related deuterocanonical books. It functions as a name rather than as a general description or action word. This name appears 148 times in the Greek LXX corpus, beginning in Exodus and continuing through 2 Maccabees. Its precise referent in any particular verse must be identified from that verse’s surrounding context.

This adjective describes someone who is guiltless—without blame or a charge of wrongdoing. It can characterize a person’s standing in relation to an accusation, judgment, or responsibility. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs 54 times, mostly in the Old Testament books, and its meaning remains centered on innocence rather than on a particular emotion or action. The surrounding verse determines whose guiltlessness is being stated and what accusation or situation is in view.

This verb means to sin through ignorance—that is, to do wrong without full awareness of the offense. It describes the act itself rather than naming a person or object. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, in Numbers 15:28. Its precise force in that passage depends on the surrounding verse and its larger discussion, but the central idea is wrongdoing committed unintentionally or without knowledge.

This verb means “hearken to” or “listen to.” It describes giving attention to what is heard, whether the emphasis is simply on listening or on listening with care. In the Greek Old Testament and related deuterocanonical books represented here, it occurs five times: once in Isaiah, once in Wisdom, and three times in Sirach. Its basic sense is receptive attention to spoken words or a message; the surrounding verse determines what is being heard and why it matters.

Alkatha is a proper name, referring to a specific place or location rather than expressing an action, quality, or general idea. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, in Joshua 19:44. Because the name is preserved as a place name and no verse text or surrounding context is provided here, its precise location or significance cannot be explained further from this word alone. Its role is therefore straightforward: Alkatha identifies a named place within the territorial record in Joshua.

Ammoni is a proper name identifying an Ammonite person or people. It functions as a personal or group designation rather than as a word describing an action, quality, or object. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs four times, in four verses, across 1 Chronicles, Ezra, and Nehemiah. The name is rendered “Ammoni,” preserving its identity as a designation connected with Ammon. The exact reference of the name in each passage depends on the surrounding verse and passage context.

This word describes an action done without mercy or compassion—“mercilessly” or “ruthlessly.” As an adverb, it tells how someone acts or treats another person. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs twice, both times in Job, showing a concentrated use rather than a broad range of occurrences. Its central idea is harshness that withholds pity, portraying conduct that is severe and unrelenting. The surrounding verse is needed to determine exactly who acts this way and how the action is expressed in each passage.

This word describes someone or something considered worthy or deserving. As an adjective, it can express that a person, action, or thing has a fitting claim to honor, value, treatment, or recognition. As a noun, it can refer to a worthy or deserving person. In the Greek Old Testament and related LXX writings, it occurs 44 times, showing regular use for evaluating worth or suitability rather than naming one specific kind of person or object.

This adjective describes a male person who has not been circumcised. In the Greek Old Testament, it is used of people and, in some passages, of groups identified by this physical condition. The word occurs 34 times in the Greek Old Testament and related deuterocanonical books, from Genesis through 1 Maccabees. Its basic meaning remains straightforward: “uncircumcised.” In some passages, the surrounding context may give this description additional covenantal or communal significance, but the word itself directly identifies the absence of circumcision.

This Greek LXX verb means “choke” or “drown”—to cause someone or something to lose breath or be overcome by water. It describes an action rather than a person, object, or quality. The word occurs once in the Greek Old Testament data, in Nahum 2:13. Because the verse text and surrounding passage are not included here, its precise force in that sentence must be understood from the immediate context. Its basic sense remains the forceful stopping of breathing, whether by choking or drowning.

This adverb means “unexpectedly” or “suddenly,” describing something that happens without being anticipated or with little warning. It focuses on the manner or timing of an event rather than naming the event itself. In the Greek LXX corpus represented here, it occurs twice, both in 2 Maccabees. Its precise force in either passage depends on the surrounding sentence, but its central idea remains an unforeseen or abrupt occurrence.

This verb means “join”: it describes bringing people or things together so they are connected or fitted together. Its basic sense is action-oriented, referring to the act of joining rather than to a person, object, or quality. In the Greek Old Testament and related LXX books, it occurs nine times, showing that it is used across several passages while retaining this central idea. Its precise force in any one verse depends on the surrounding context.

This adjective means “sick,” describing someone whose health is impaired or who is physically unwell. In the LXX material represented here, it occurs twice: once in Malachi and once in Sirach. Its basic sense remains direct and concrete, while the surrounding sentence determines exactly whom or what it describes. The same English rendering, “sick,” is used in both recorded occurrences.

“Without food” is the meaning of this adverb. It modifies a statement to indicate that food is absent or not being taken, rather than naming a person, object, or place. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, in Job 24:6. The word-level entry does not include the verse text or surrounding passage, so its exact force there must be understood from that context. Its central idea remains the absence of food in the situation described.

This word means “constellation,” referring to a recognizable arrangement of stars in the sky. It is a noun naming a heavenly formation rather than an action or quality. In the Greek Old Testament and deuterocanonical books represented here, it occurs 35 times, showing that it is used across several biblical writings when referring to the starry heavens. Its precise significance in any particular verse depends on the surrounding context.

Atipha is a proper name, also rendered Atifa. It identifies an individual rather than describing an action, quality, or object. In the Greek Old Testament, this name occurs once, in Nehemiah 7:56. The available wording preserves the name but does not provide a separate definition or explain its etymology. Its precise significance in that passage must therefore be understood from the surrounding verse and its wider context.

This noun means “obscurity,” referring to a condition of being hidden, unclear, or difficult to see. It describes darkness or a loss of clarity rather than a person, action, or object. In the Greek Old Testament, the word occurs 53 times, with most occurrences in the Old Testament and a few in the deuterocanonical books. Its precise force in any particular verse depends on the surrounding wording, but its central idea remains obscurity or lack of clear visibility.

This adjective describes someone or something that is without fear. It presents the absence of fear as the defining quality, rather than naming a particular emotion, action, or event. In the Greek Old Testament and related writings represented here, it occurs four times, so its basic meaning remains consistent while its precise force depends on the sentence and surrounding passage. The word is found in Proverbs, Wisdom, and Sirach, showing that it can describe a condition or manner of being marked by freedom from fear.

Achia, also rendered Akhia, is a personal name used for people in the Greek Old Testament. It identifies individuals rather than describing an action, quality, or object. The name occurs 21 times across 17 verses, from 1 Samuel through 2 Chronicles, with most occurrences in 1 Kings. Since the name itself is the meaning supplied for this word, its significance in any particular passage comes from the person being named and the surrounding biblical context.

Achinoom is a proper name—the personal name of a woman mentioned in the Greek Old Testament. It identifies a particular person rather than describing an object, action, quality, or general idea. The name appears four times in the Greek Old Testament, in 1 Samuel and 2 Samuel. Because it functions as a name, its meaning here is primarily identification: it distinguishes this woman from other people in the narrative. The English rendering is “Achinoom,” also written “Akhinoom.”

Baithgedōr is a proper name, also rendered “Vethyethor.” It identifies a particular named entity rather than describing an action, quality, or general idea. In the Greek Old Testament, this name occurs one time, in 1 Chronicles 2:51. The available lexical information gives the name itself but does not provide enough surrounding verse text to explain whom or what it identifies there. Its precise significance therefore belongs to the context of that passage.

Belga, also rendered Velga, is a proper name rather than a general word describing an object, action, or quality. In the Greek Old Testament, it identifies a person or family by name. The name occurs once in the LXX, at 1 Chronicles 24:14, and its precise historical identity must be understood from that passage and its surrounding context. No broader lexical meaning is provided beyond these name forms.

This Greek LXX noun means “small cluster,” referring to a compact group of items gathered closely together. It occurs once in the Greek Old Testament, at Isaiah 18:5. The word’s basic sense is therefore narrow and concrete: it identifies a small, clustered quantity rather than a large mass or scattered collection. Its exact force in that verse depends on the surrounding passage, but the word itself points to something gathered into a small cluster.

This word describes something made of fine linen, a high-quality textile used for clothing, coverings, and other decorated furnishings. It is an adjective, so it identifies the material or quality of an object rather than naming the object itself. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs 16 times in 13 verses, including descriptions connected with garments and furnishings. Its central meaning remains consistent: linen distinguished by its fineness or quality. The precise force in any particular passage depends on the object it describes and the surrounding wording.

Gamul is a proper name, rendered as “Gamul,” rather than a word describing an action, quality, or object. In the Greek Old Testament, it identifies a particular person named Gamul. This name occurs once, in 1 Chronicles 24:17. Without the verse text and surrounding passage, its personal significance cannot be explained further; its clear lexical function is to designate an individual by name.

In the Greek Old Testament, Γεθθαιμ is a proper name rendered “Geththaim” or “Yeththem.” It functions as a name rather than a general word describing an action, quality, or object. The name occurs four times in the LXX, appearing in Genesis 36:35, 2 Samuel 4:3, 1 Chronicles 1:46, and Job 42:17. Without the surrounding verse text, these references establish where the name occurs but do not by themselves identify whether it refers to a person, place, or another named entity.

This noun means “grape-stone,” referring to the hard seed found inside a grape. It names a small physical part of the grape rather than an action, person, or quality. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, in Numbers 6:4, within the description of what a Nazirite was forbidden to eat. The word’s basic meaning remains specific and concrete: a grape seed or stone.

This noun means a petition: a request presented to someone for help, favor, or action. It refers to the request itself rather than to the person making it or the response given. In the Greek Old Testament and related LXX writings, it is used 76 times, showing a recurring term for an expressed request. Its precise force in any particular verse depends on the surrounding passage, but the central idea remains a petition directed toward another person or authority.

This verb means “mark out by lines” or “delineate,” describing the act of tracing boundaries, outlines, or divisions so that something is clearly defined. It can refer to setting out a shape or area in a visible, organized way. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs nine times, especially in Ezekiel, where clear outlining is associated with describing or presenting dimensions and arrangements. Its precise force in any particular verse depends on what is being outlined.

This verb means to form something perfectly, expressing careful or complete shaping rather than merely making it. It appears once in the Greek Old Testament, the Septuagint, at Wisdom 19:6. Because the verse text and surrounding context are not included here, the word’s precise force in that passage cannot be described further; its lexical sense remains the idea of bringing something into a fully formed state. It functions as a verb.

gl: one who is at variance; dissenter
d: one who is at variance; dissenter

e.t: This adjective describes someone who is at variance with others—a dissenter rather than a person in agreement. It identifies a person marked by disagreement or opposition, but the lexical sense does not by itself explain the reason for that disagreement or the surrounding situation. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, at Proverbs 33:20; understanding its precise force there requires the verse and its surrounding passage.

This Greek LXX noun means “dogma” or “decree”: an established ruling, order, or authoritative instruction. It can describe a formal command issued for people to follow, rather than a passing suggestion. The word occurs six times in the Greek LXX corpus, including Daniel and the Maccabean books. Its exact force in any verse depends on the surrounding sentence, but its central idea remains an officially stated decree or settled rule.

Doudi, also rendered Thuthi, is a proper name referring to a person. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, at 2 Samuel 23:24. The name itself identifies an individual rather than expressing an action, quality, or general idea. Because the verse text and surrounding context are not included here, the person’s role or significance cannot be described from the name alone.

This noun means “misfortune”—an unfortunate event or difficult condition that brings trouble or loss. It names hardship as something experienced, rather than describing a person’s character or an action they perform. In the Greek LXX corpus represented here, it occurs once, in 2 Maccabees 5:20. Its precise force in that passage depends on the surrounding verse and context, which are not included here.

This word means “internal organs,” referring to the parts within an animal’s body. It is an adjective that describes those inner bodily parts rather than naming a person, action, or emotion. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs twice, both times in Leviticus 1, where its meaning belongs to descriptions of sacrificial animals. Its precise force in either verse is understood through the surrounding wording, but the basic reference remains the animal’s inward organs.

The word means “if” or “whether.” It introduces a condition, possibility, or question, connecting one statement with another rather than naming a person, thing, or action. In the Greek Old Testament and deuterocanonical books, it appears 946 times, so readers may encounter it in many kinds of sentences. Its precise force depends on the surrounding sentence: it can present something as conditional (“if”) or frame an alternative or uncertainty (“whether”).

This adjective describes someone who shows mercy: treating others with compassion rather than harshness. It can describe a person or characterize what that person does. In the Greek Old Testament and related Greek writings represented here, the word is rendered “merciful” and occurs 26 times, so it expresses a recurring description of compassionate character. Its central sense remains focused on kindness, pity, and a willingness to withhold deserved severity.

Eliareph, also written Eliaref, is a proper name rather than a word that describes an action, quality, or object. In the Greek Old Testament (LXX), it appears once, at 1 Kings 4:3. The available lexical information identifies the name itself but does not provide a further definition or description of the person. Its significance in that passage must be understood from the surrounding verse and context.

This Greek LXX verb means to fasten something with a brooch or clasp. It describes the act of securing clothing or another item by using such a fastening, rather than merely being near or wearing it. The word occurs once in the Greek LXX corpus, in 3 Maccabees 7:5. Its precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its basic meaning remains the practical action of fastening with a brooch.

This Greek LXX adjective describes something as “still in the night,” emphasizing the nighttime setting or condition. It is a descriptive word rather than a name or action, so it tells the reader when something is taking place or remains. The word occurs once in the Greek LXX corpus, in 3 Maccabees 5:5. Its precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding wording, but its basic sense is a quiet or continuing state associated with the night.

This noun means “appeasement” or “propitiation”: an act or offering intended to settle offense and restore acceptance. It describes a recognized means of dealing with guilt or estrangement, especially in the Old Testament and deuterocanonical Greek writings. The word occurs 15 times in the Greek Old Testament corpus, including passages in Exodus, Leviticus, Ezekiel, Sirach, and 2 Maccabees. Its precise force in any particular verse depends on the surrounding passage.

This Greek LXX noun refers to a festival or holiday—a designated occasion set apart for celebration. It names the observance itself rather than describing a person, action, or quality. The word occurs once in the Greek Old Testament collection represented here, in Wisdom 19:16. Since the surrounding verse text is not included, that reference does not by itself show the particular emphasis of the occasion. Its basic meaning remains a festival or holiday, with the surrounding passage determining how the observance functions in that sentence.

This word refers to an arbiter or umpire—someone who helps judge between parties or settle a matter. It can function as a noun for such a person or as a descriptive word for someone serving in that role. In the Greek Old Testament, it appears four times, all in Proverbs, so its central idea is a person associated with impartial judgment and dispute resolution. The surrounding verse determines the specific situation in which this judging role is relevant.

This Greek LXX noun means “march,” referring to the act of moving forward from one place to another. It names a movement or advance rather than the person who travels or the action of leading. The word occurs once in the Greek LXX corpus, in 3 Maccabees 3:14. Without the verse text, its precise force in that passage cannot be described more narrowly, but its basic meaning is a march or advancing movement.

This Greek LXX verb means “give way; yield.” It describes an action in which a person or party gives way rather than continuing to resist or maintain a position. The word appears twice in the Greek LXX, both times in 2 Maccabees. Its basic sense is therefore straightforward: to yield, make room, or concede instead of pressing forward or holding firm. The surrounding sentence determines precisely what or whom the person yields to.

Esēlebbōn, also rendered Esilevvon, is a proper name rather than a word describing an action, quality, or object. In the Greek Old Testament, it identifies a person named Eselebbon. This name occurs once, in 1 Chronicles 4:3. Because the surrounding verse text is not included here, the name itself does not provide further information about the person’s identity, family, role, or significance. Its ordinary function is simply to name an individual in that genealogical setting.

This adjective means “innermost,” describing something located at the deepest or most interior point rather than near the outside. It identifies an inward position or the furthest part within something. In the Greek Old Testament, this word occurs once, in Job 28:18. Its precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding wording, but its basic meaning remains a description of what lies furthest inside.

This adjective describes someone acting “cheerfully” or “stimulatedly,” expressing an encouraged, lively spirit. It describes the manner in which a person acts, rather than naming a person or object. In the Greek LXX corpus, it occurs once, in 2 Maccabees 11:26. Its precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its basic sense points to willing, energetic cheerfulness.

This word means “celebration”—an expression or occasion of gladness and rejoicing. As a noun in the Greek Old Testament, it refers to joyful celebration rather than to an action someone performs. It is used 154 times in the LXX, appearing in descriptions of communal joy, festive occasions, and glad responses. Its broad use across the Old Testament and deuterocanonical books shows that celebration can mark worship, public gatherings, and personal rejoicing. The surrounding passage determines the particular reason for the celebration in any given verse.

Ephra, also rendered Efra, is a proper name identifying a person in the Greek Old Testament. It occurs once, at 1 Kings 4:6. Because this is a personal name rather than a descriptive word, its basic meaning is the individual named Ephra; the surrounding verse is needed to explain that person’s specific role or connection in the passage. The name itself does not express an action, quality, command, or spiritual concept.

This LXX verb means “boil”: to cook or heat something in liquid until it reaches a boiling state. It describes an action rather than an object or person. The word occurs 23 times in the Greek Old Testament and related Greek biblical books, including passages concerning food preparation and cooking, though the precise force in any verse depends on its surrounding wording. Its normal sense remains straightforward: bringing food or another substance to a boil.

Zabou, also rendered Zavu, is a personal name rather than a word describing an action, quality, or object. It identifies an individual in the Greek Old Testament tradition. This name occurs twice in the LXX corpus: once in Ezra 10:28 and once in Nehemiah 3:20. Without the surrounding verse text, its particular family connection or role cannot be explained here; the lexical evidence establishes the name itself and its use as a proper name.

This adjective describes something as “still” or “quiet.” It can characterize a person, condition, or setting marked by the absence of disturbance or activity. In the LXX corpus represented here, it occurs twice: once in Wisdom and once in Sirach. One English rendering is “quiet,” which fits the central sense. The surrounding verse determines whether the word emphasizes calmness, silence, or lack of movement, but its basic idea remains peaceful stillness rather than agitation.

This adjective describes something as worse in quality or condition, or less in amount, degree, or standing. It can compare one person, thing, or situation with another, showing that the first falls short of the second. In the Greek Old Testament and related Greek writings, it occurs 13 times, including passages from 1 Samuel, Job, Isaiah, and the Wisdom literature. Its precise force in a particular verse depends on what is being compared.

This Greek LXX noun means “heap”: a gathered mass or collection brought together in one place. It names something viewed as a group or mound rather than as separate individual pieces. The word occurs seven times in the Greek LXX corpus, across passages from Exodus, Job, Zephaniah, Sirach, 1 Maccabees, and Song of Songs. Its precise significance in any particular verse comes from what has been gathered and the surrounding sentence.

gl: written with one’s own hand; genuine
d: written with one’s own hand; genuine

e.t: This adjective means “written with one’s own hand” and, by extension, “genuine.” It describes something presented as authentic rather than falsely attributed or copied. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, in Psalm 151:1, so its ordinary meaning is clear even though the surrounding verse text is not included here. The related rendering “genuine” highlights the word’s emphasis on authenticity and trustworthy origin.

This proper noun refers to a person from Jerusalem—a “Hierosolymite” or “Ierosolimitis.” It functions as a personal designation rather than a general description of an action, quality, or object. In the LXX corpus represented here, it occurs three times: once in Sirach and twice in 4 Maccabees. The word identifies someone by connection with Jerusalem, while the surrounding verse determines what that person is doing or saying.

Iettour, also rendered Iettur, is a proper name identifying a person rather than describing an action, quality, or object. It occurs once in the Greek Old Testament, in 1 Chronicles 1:31. Because names identify individuals, the word’s basic meaning is its role as that person’s name; the surrounding genealogy supplies the specific identity in that passage. The name itself does not provide a general teaching or abstract definition.

This Greek LXX verb means to have means or to have force. It describes possessing the resources, ability, or strength needed to accomplish something, and can also describe having effective power. It is a verb, so it expresses what someone has or is able to exert rather than naming a person or thing. In the Greek Old Testament and related deuterocanonical books, it occurs 87 times, showing regular use for capability or force. Its precise sense in a particular verse depends on the surrounding sentence.

This word is a proper name, rendered “Kainaios; Keneos.” It identifies a person or people by name rather than describing an action, quality, or object. In the Greek Old Testament (LXX), it occurs once, in Genesis 15:19. Because it is a name and no wider usage is recorded in this corpus, its precise reference depends on the surrounding passage rather than on a broader range of meanings.

This word means “furnace,” a heated structure used as a place of intense fire. It is a noun that names the furnace itself rather than the act of heating or burning. In the Greek Old Testament and related Greek writings represented here, it occurs 44 times, showing that this is a regularly used term for such a place. The word appears in passages from Genesis, Deuteronomy, Jeremiah, Ezekiel, Daniel, and other books, including both Old Testament and deuterocanonical material.

This noun refers to a powerful storm, especially a squall descending from above or a hurricane. It presents the storm as sudden and forceful, emphasizing the violent movement of wind and weather rather than an ordinary breeze or gentle rain. In the Greek Old Testament and related Greek writings, the word occurs 28 times, showing that it is used repeatedly for severe atmospheric forces. Its precise force in any verse depends on the surrounding passage.

This Greek LXX noun means “lodging”: a place where someone stays or finds accommodation. It refers to a temporary dwelling or guest place rather than identifying a person or action. The word occurs 13 times in the Greek Old Testament and related deuterocanonical books represented here, including passages in Exodus, Samuel, Chronicles, Jeremiah, and 1 Maccabees. Its precise force in any particular verse depends on the surrounding sentence, but its central idea remains a place of lodging or temporary stay.

This Greek LXX noun means “curse”: a spoken or declared judgment that brings harm, rejection, or consequences upon someone or something. It is used for the opposite of blessing and for the condition or pronouncement associated with being cursed. The word occurs 40 times in the Greek Old Testament and related deuterocanonical books, including frequent use in Deuteronomy. Its exact force in a particular verse depends on the surrounding passage.

This Greek LXX verb means “retain; detain”: to hold onto something or keep someone from leaving. It can describe preserving what is held or restraining a person, depending on the sentence. The word appears 50 times in the Greek Old Testament and related LXX writings, so its basic idea is broad but consistently concerns holding, keeping, or preventing release. Its precise force in any verse depends on what is being held and the surrounding context.

This noun refers to dozing or sleep—the state of resting or being asleep. Its central meaning is straightforward and is rendered as “sleep” in one recorded translation. In the Greek LXX corpus represented here, it occurs twice, both in Sirach. The word itself names the condition of sleep rather than an action, person, or abstract quality. Its precise force in either passage depends on the surrounding verse and context.

This word means “bedroom,” referring to a room used for sleeping or private rest. It is a noun naming a particular place within a house or dwelling, rather than an action or quality. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs nine times across nine verses, showing a clear, concrete household meaning. Its precise significance in any particular verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its ordinary sense remains a bedroom or sleeping room.

This word means “lily,” the name of a flowering plant. It is a noun used for the plant itself, including when lilies are mentioned in descriptions of created things, furnishings, or beauty. In the Greek Old Testament corpus, it occurs 47 times, so it is a recurring concrete word rather than a rare expression. Its precise significance in any particular verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its central meaning remains the lily flower.

This noun means “leprosy,” referring to the condition named in the Greek Old Testament. It is used as a label for this condition rather than as an action or description of a person’s character. The word occurs 40 times in the Greek Old Testament, with most occurrences in Leviticus, especially the passages concerned with examining and identifying it. Its basic meaning remains “leprosy,” while the surrounding verse determines how the condition is being discussed.

Loudiim is a proper name for a people or family group; “Luthim” is another supplied rendering of the same name. It is not a common word describing an action, quality, or object, but a designation for a named people. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, in Genesis 10:13. The name’s precise historical or contextual significance must be understood from the surrounding passage rather than from the name alone.

This Greek LXX word is a proper name, rendered in the lexical definition as “Makēdan; Makithan.” It identifies a specific named entity rather than expressing an action, quality, or general idea. The word occurs once in the Greek LXX corpus, in Joshua 15:41. Because the verse text and surrounding context are not available here, the name itself does not establish whether the reference is to a place, person, or another named entity. Its precise identification depends on the passage where it appears.

“Fade” is a verb describing the loss of strength, freshness, or visible force, as something gradually becomes less than it was. It names a process of diminishing rather than a sudden change. In the Greek LXX, this word occurs four times, twice in Job and twice in Wisdom, so its basic sense is concise but used across both books. The surrounding verse determines what is fading in each occurrence.

Meazoth is a proper name, rendered consistently as “Meazoth” in the Greek Old Testament. It does not function as a common word describing an action, quality, or object; rather, it identifies a named entity in the text. This name occurs twice in the Septuagint, both times in 1 Chronicles, at 1 Chronicles 25:4 and 25:30. Its precise referent is determined by the surrounding passage.

This noun means “bee house; beehive,” referring to a place where bees live or gather. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs three times, in Judges and 1 Samuel, and is rendered with reference to bees in each recorded occurrence. The word identifies the bees’ dwelling rather than describing a person, action, or spiritual quality. Its exact force in any particular verse is best understood from the surrounding passage.

Misael is a proper name identifying a person, rendered here as “Misaēl” or “Misel.” It is not a common word describing an action, quality, object, or idea. In the Greek Old Testament and related Greek writings, the name appears 12 times, including several references in Daniel and Nehemiah. Its meaning as a personal name is best preserved by recognizing the individual it identifies in each passage; the surrounding verse supplies the specific context.

Mallow is the name of a plant. This word is a noun, so it identifies the plant itself rather than describing an action or quality. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, in Job 24:24. Its basic meaning is therefore straightforward: it refers to mallow, a plant mentioned by name in that passage. The precise significance of the reference depends on the surrounding verse and passage, which are not included here.

This word means “of me” or “mine,” expressing a relationship to the speaker. It is a pronoun used when someone identifies a person or thing as belonging to, coming from, or being associated with “me.” Its exact English wording depends on the sentence: it may describe possession, connection, or origin. In the Greek LXX corpus, it occurs 4,182 times, showing that this is a common way to point back to the speaker. It appears throughout the Old Testament and deuterocanonical books represented in the LXX.

This Greek LXX verb means “initiate” or “learn the secret,” describing someone being brought into knowledge that was previously hidden. It can refer to entering an understanding or receiving instruction in something not openly known. The word appears once in the Greek LXX corpus, in 3 Maccabees 2:30. Its precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its basic sense concerns being initiated into secret or special knowledge.

This Greek LXX adjective means “new” or “young.” It describes something recent or someone who is youthful, with the surrounding noun showing which sense applies. The word appears 119 times in the Greek Old Testament and deuterocanonical books, so it can describe both newly made or renewed things and people who are not yet mature in age. Its basic idea is freshness, newness, or youth rather than something old or established.

This word means “armament” or “weapon”—equipment used for fighting or defense. It is a noun describing a weapon or a set of weapons rather than the act of fighting itself. In the Greek Old Testament and related Greek writings represented here, it occurs 65 times, showing regular use for military equipment. Its range includes weapons carried by individuals and weapons prepared for wider defense, while the surrounding verse determines the particular kind intended.

This noun means “panoply” or “full armor”—the complete set of protective equipment prepared for battle. It refers not merely to one weapon or piece of protection, but to armor considered as a whole. In the Greek Old Testament and related Greek writings represented here, it occurs 10 times, including passages about warriors, battle, and protective equipment. Its precise force in any particular verse depends on the surrounding context, but the central idea remains a complete suit or array of armor.

e.t: This adjective means “of every kind; of all sorts.” It describes something as varied or inclusive, covering different kinds rather than belonging to only one category. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, in Job 40:21, so its ordinary meaning is clear even though the surrounding verse text is not provided here. The word functions as a broad descriptive term, emphasizing variety or the inclusion of multiple kinds. Its exact force in Job depends on the sentence and passage where it appears.

This Greek LXX noun means “virginal” or “virgin,” referring to a female who is sexually untouched or describing virginity. It is used for people in passages throughout the Greek Old Testament and related deuterocanonical books. The word occurs 61 times in this LXX corpus, so its precise significance in any particular verse depends on the surrounding passage. Its basic sense remains focused on virginity or a virginal state.

This Greek LXX verb describes falling amid something or becoming caught in the midst of it. Its central idea is movement into an surrounding situation rather than simply falling in isolation. The word appears nine times in the Greek Old Testament and related Greek writings represented here, including four occurrences in the Old Testament and five in deuterocanonical books. Its exact force in any passage depends on what the person or thing falls amid.

Pikran is a proper name preserved in the Greek Old Testament and related Greek Jewish writings. Its supplied meaning is simply “Pikran”; the available lexical information does not identify whether it names a person, place, or something else. The word occurs four times in the LXX corpus: three times in Old Testament books and once in Sirach. Its exact reference in any passage must be understood from that passage’s surrounding text.

This adjective means “for harlots,” describing something associated with or intended for harlots. It functions as a descriptive word rather than naming a person or action by itself. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs twice, in Proverbs 7:10 and Ezekiel 16:24. Those references show that the word belongs to language concerning harlots, while the surrounding verse determines exactly what object or setting it describes in each passage.

This Greek LXX noun means “foraging” or a “foraging expedition”—an organized search or outing to gather provisions, especially in a military setting. It describes the activity itself rather than the people carrying it out. The word occurs 38 times in the Greek Old Testament and related LXX corpus, appearing especially in historical and prophetic books. Its precise force in any particular verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its central idea remains a deliberate expedition to collect supplies or spoil.

This verb means “rehearse” or “relate”: to recount something by telling it again or reporting it. It describes the act of presenting an account, rather than naming a person, object, or quality. In the Greek LXX corpus represented here, it occurs once, at 2 Maccabees 8:19. The precise force of the verb in that passage depends on the surrounding verse and passage, but its basic sense is to recount or report what has happened or been said.

This Greek LXX verb means “propose”: to put something forward for consideration, appointment, or action. It describes the act of presenting a person or thing before others rather than merely thinking about it privately. The word occurs 12 times in the Greek Old Testament and related Greek writings represented in this corpus, including passages from Exodus, Leviticus, Psalms, and the Maccabean books. Its precise force in any individual verse depends on what is being put forward and the surrounding sentence.

Sauchites, also rendered Safkhitis, is a proper name identifying a person in the Greek Old Testament. It does not describe an action, quality, or general idea; it functions as a personal designation. The name occurs four times in the Greek text of Job, and each occurrence belongs to that book. Its precise role in any particular verse depends on the surrounding passage, but the word itself is simply the person’s name.

Semma is a proper name, referring to a person rather than describing an action, quality, or general object. In the Greek Old Testament, it appears once, in 1 Chronicles 7:37. The available lexical information identifies the name itself but does not provide a further meaning or description. Therefore, Semma should be understood simply as the personal name preserved in that genealogical record.

Sessi is a proper name, referring to a named individual in the Greek Old Testament. It is rendered as “Sessi” and does not describe an action, quality, or general object. This name occurs twice in the Greek Old Testament corpus, once in Numbers 13:22 and once in Judges 1:10. The name itself identifies someone, while the surrounding verse supplies the person’s specific role or situation.

This Greek LXX verb means “keep silent”: to remain quiet or refrain from speaking. It describes silence as an action, whether someone deliberately stops speaking or stays quiet in a situation. The word appears 14 times in the Greek LXX corpus, across books including Exodus, Psalms, Sirach, Amos, and 1 Maccabees. Its exact force in any verse depends on the surrounding words, but its central sense remains the choice or condition of being silent.

This verb means “keep watch” or “watch closely,” describing attentive observation of a person, place, or situation. It expresses more than merely looking; it points to sustained attention and careful notice. In the Greek Old Testament translation, it appears seven times, including passages involving people watching and passages describing God’s eyes observing human ways. Its precise force in any particular verse depends on what or whom the subject is watching, but the central idea remains alert, focused observation.

Sobnia, also rendered Sovnia, is a proper name rather than a word describing an action, quality, or object. It identifies a person or named individual in the Greek Old Testament tradition. This name occurs once in the LXX corpus, at 1 Chronicles 15:24. Without the surrounding verse text, Scripture does not provide enough information here to explain the person’s role or significance beyond identifying the name itself.

This adjective means “commensurate with,” describing something that corresponds to or is proportionate to something else. It expresses a fitting relationship in measure, size, or suitability rather than simply identifying an object. In the Greek LXX, it occurs once, in Jeremiah 22:14. The precise force of the word in that verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its normal sense is that one thing matches or is suitably measured against another.

This word refers to “consciousness” or “conscience”—a person’s inward awareness, especially the inner sense that recognizes or responds to what is right or wrong. It is a noun describing an inward faculty rather than an outward action. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs twice: once in Ecclesiastes and once in Wisdom. Its precise force in either passage depends on the surrounding verse and context.

This verb means “go,” describing movement from one place or situation to another. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, in Proverbs 22:10. Its basic sense is straightforward: someone goes or departs. The surrounding wording is needed to determine who is moving and what destination or circumstance is involved in that verse. The word itself expresses the act of going rather than a particular attitude, purpose, or spiritual lesson.

Sōstratos is a personal name, referring to a particular man rather than describing an action, quality, or object. It appears twice in the Greek Old Testament collection, both times in 2 Maccabees, at 2 Maccabees 4:28 and 4:29. As a proper name, its basic role is to identify the same named individual in those passages. The name itself does not provide a general concept or instruction; understanding what the person does in either verse requires the surrounding passage.

This Greek LXX verb means “pick”: it describes the act of picking something. It is a concise action word rather than a noun or title. The word occurs three times in the Greek Old Testament, in Ezra, Isaiah, and Daniel. Its precise force in any one passage depends on what is being picked and the surrounding sentence, but its central meaning remains the act of picking. The word’s lexical meaning is directly identified as “pick.”

This noun means a wound: an injury or damaged place caused by harm. In the Greek Old Testament and deuterocanonical books, it is used for bodily hurt rather than an action or person. It occurs 14 times in the LXX, across 13 verses, from Genesis through 2 Maccabees. The same basic meaning appears in passages from Exodus, Job, and Isaiah, where the word is rendered “wound.”

This Greek LXX noun means “dish,” referring to a vessel or serving piece. It appears 19 times in the Greek Old Testament and related LXX writings, with most occurrences in Numbers. The word is used for a recognizable household or worship-related vessel, but its precise use in any particular passage depends on the surrounding verse. Its first recorded occurrence is Exodus 25:29, and it also appears in Numbers and Sirach.

This Greek LXX verb means “lie,” describing something that is positioned or situated in a place. It expresses being there rather than an action of speaking falsely. The word occurs twice in the Greek Old Testament, once in Proverbs and once in Ezekiel. Its precise force in either passage depends on the surrounding wording, but its basic sense is simply to lie or be situated. [p03:word:lxx:L713145:identity] [p03:word:lxx:L713145:occurrences]

Phalai, also rendered Fale, is a proper name rather than a word describing an action, quality, or object. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, at Nehemiah 10:25. Because the available information identifies the person by name but does not provide the verse text or surrounding passage, the name itself does not establish additional meaning or significance. Its precise role in Nehemiah depends on the context of that passage. The name is preserved as a distinct Greek LXX form and should not be treated as an ordinary descriptive term.

This Greek noun means “watch-post; garrisoned fort”—a defended place established for guarding an area. It refers to a military position or stronghold rather than to the act of watching itself. The word occurs three times in the Greek LXX corpus, all in 2 Maccabees, at 10:32, 10:33, and 13:19. Its precise significance in any one passage depends on the surrounding account, but its ordinary sense is a fortified location held for protection or defense.

This adjective means “green,” describing the color of living plants, vegetation, or other things with a fresh green appearance. It is used in the Greek Old Testament to identify something by its visible color rather than to express an abstract quality. The word occurs 15 times across 14 Old Testament verses, including descriptions connected with plants and vegetation. Its precise force in any particular verse depends on the surrounding context.

This word means “stringed instrument,” referring to a musical instrument played with strings. As a noun, it names the instrument itself rather than the act of playing or the music produced. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs 20 times, with half of those occurrences in Psalms, showing its recurring place in descriptions of musical praise and worship. Its earliest listed occurrence is Genesis 4:21, and its latest is Sirach 40:21. The precise role of the instrument in any particular passage depends on the surrounding verse and context.

This word is a proper name: “Ōrōnēn; Oronin.” It identifies a person named Oronin rather than describing an action, quality, or object. In the Greek Old Testament (LXX), it occurs once, at 2 Samuel 13:34. Because the verse text and surrounding passage are not included here, the name itself supplies the identification, while the passage provides the person’s specific role in that account.
